summary:
Cundinamarca is a department of Colombia, and it stands directly under the national legal framework. None of the sources in the record carries a finding on law, enforcement practice or recorded incidents specific to this department, so a visitor's expectations rest on how Colombian national rules apply and on the enforcement record documented elsewhere in the country.

Legal gender recognition runs through an administrative channel rather than a court. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. A person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate since 1993, with current options of F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero); the process is notarial, requires no surgery and no court ruling, and the sources state that it applies equally in Cundinamarca. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement.

Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request and a simultaneous name change free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the non-binary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

The favourable legal framework sits alongside lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, drowning in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, after being thrown in unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was", President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. Reporting of 6 August 2025 covers the wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people that followed the Millerey killing and offers no content specific to Cundinamarca.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have circulated flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was given one week to leave town or be killed and forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. An activist quoted in the investigation says the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases; 41 trans women were killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
The violence baseline against which Cundinamarca is assessed is national and organised rather than incidental. Armed-group flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá name individuals for killing, and killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Recorded totals diverge by source and period: 41 trans women killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders recorded by the Attorney General's Office between January and May 2025. The Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 and the CNN report of 6 August 2025 both contain no Cundinamarca-specific information.

Implementation gaps are documented at the administrative level. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans in Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 mission found a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.
